title: “JUDGE NOT.” THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES—UNTIL YOU READ WHAT JESUS SAID NEXT
paragraphs: “JUDGE NOT.” THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES—UNTIL YOU READ WHAT JESUS SAID NEXT
Matthew 7:1 was never permission to call darkness light. It was a warning that before you reach for someone else’s speck, you had better let Jesus deal with the plank in your own eye.
There is a sentence people love to throw at Christians.
Sometimes it comes from a friend.
Sometimes from a comment section.
Sometimes from someone who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Sometimes from a person who simply does not want anyone questioning the direction of their life.
“Judge not.”
Two words.
Conversation over.
Or so it seems.
Because Jesus did say something very close to those words.
In Matthew 7:1, the Greek text reads:
Μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε.
Mē krinete, hina mē krithēte.
“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”
And if we stop there, it can sound absolute.
Never evaluate.
Never confront.
Never identify sin.
Never warn someone.
Never distinguish truth from error.
Never say that something is morally wrong.
Just love everybody, affirm everything, and keep your mouth closed.
There is only one problem.
Jesus did not stop speaking at verse 1.
And sometimes the most dangerous way to misunderstand Jesus is to quote His words accurately while cutting Him off before He finishes the sentence.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because Matthew 7:1 is not merely a verse about how you look at other people.
It is a mirror.
And before this article is finished, you may discover that the person Jesus is asking you to examine first is not the sinner you have been criticizing.
It is you.

The Greek verb translated “judge” comes from κρίνω — krinō. Depending on context, the word can carry senses such as judging, deciding, evaluating, or passing judgment. That matters because Scripture itself shows that not every act of moral discernment is forbidden.
Jesus is not commanding His disciples to become morally blind.
He is confronting something far more sinister.
The kind of judgment that can see everybody else’s sin while remaining strangely blind to its own.
Listen to what He says next:
“For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you.”
Then Jesus paints an almost ridiculous picture.
Why do you notice the tiny speck in your brother’s eye while ignoring the massive beam sticking out of your own?
Imagine it.
A man walking toward his brother saying, “Hold still. There is something in your eye.”
Meanwhile, a wooden beam is protruding from his own face.
He cannot see properly.
He cannot approach properly.
He may even injure the person he claims he is trying to help.
Then Jesus uses a word we should not rush past:
ὑποκριτά — hypokrita.
“Hypocrite.”
That is the heart of the warning.
Jesus is exposing hypocrisy.
He is confronting the terrifying human ability to become intensely sensitive to another person’s failure while becoming remarkably tolerant of our own.
Their anger is sinful.
Our anger is justified.
Their gossip is wicked.
We were only “telling somebody so they could pray.”
Their pride is disgusting.
Ours is confidence.
Their greed is materialism.
Ours is ambition.
Their sexual sin deserves confrontation.
Our secret lust apparently deserves another excuse.
Their marriage problems prove they need God.
Ours are complicated.
Their children are rebellious because the parents failed.
Our children are simply “going through a season.”
Their church hurt has made them bitter.
Our church hurt gives us permission to speak poison.
Their compromise is evidence that they are lukewarm.
Our compromise?
We have a reason.
And suddenly Matthew 7 is no longer ammunition for an argument.
It is surgery.
Because Jesus does not merely expose the sin of judging.
He exposes the scandal of unequal scales.
We can become prosecutors when examining another person's life and defense attorneys when examining our own.
That is what Christ destroys here.
But notice something extremely important.
Jesus does not say:
“You have a plank in your eye, therefore you can never help your brother with his speck.”
Read what He actually says:
“First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.”
First.
That word changes everything.
Repentance comes first.
Self-examination comes first.
Humility comes first.
Grace comes first.
Then, with clearer vision, you may actually be able to help your brother.
Jesus is not abolishing discernment.
He is purifying the discerner.
He is not saying sin should never be confronted.
He is saying the person confronting it must first stand beneath the same holy light of God.
Before you expose someone, ask God to expose you.
Before you correct someone, ask whether Scripture has corrected you.
Before you talk about their marriage, examine yours.
Before you condemn their parenting, examine your heart toward your own children.
Before you post about another Christian’s failure, ask whether you secretly enjoy being the one who knows.
Before you call somebody a hypocrite...
make sure you have heard Jesus whisper the word toward your own heart.
That changes the tone of Christian correction completely.
And the rest of Scripture confirms that Christians are not commanded to abandon moral discernment.
Later in Matthew 7, Jesus warns about false prophets and says they will be recognized “by their fruits.” Recognition requires discernment.
In John 7:24, Jesus says:
“Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”

Paul tells believers in Galatians 6:1 that if someone is caught in transgression, those who are spiritual should restore that person in a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
That is almost the heartbeat of Matthew 7 in another form.
See the sin.
Do not pretend it is righteousness.
But approach the sinner remembering that you are made of the same fallen dust.
Restore.
Do not enjoy destroying.
Speak truth.
Do not weaponize truth.
Correct.
Do not humiliate.
Discern.
Do not play God.
There is an enormous difference between saying, “What you are doing contradicts Scripture,” and saying, “You are beyond the mercy of God.”
One may be biblical discernment.
The other attempts to sit in a chair that belongs to God alone.

Christians are called to recognize good and evil. We are commanded to test teaching. We are commanded to pursue holiness. There are even circumstances in which church discipline is biblically required.
But nowhere are Christians given permission to become self-righteous executioners of people Christ may still be pursuing.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Her sin was real.
Jesus did not rename adultery as authenticity.
He did not tell everyone that moral truth was subjective.
He showed astonishing mercy, and then He called her away from sin.
Grace and truth were not enemies in Jesus.
They met perfectly in Him.
That matters because our generation often offers us two counterfeit choices.
Condemn people without mercy.
Or affirm people without truth.
Jesus does neither.
He can look directly at sin without looking away from the sinner.
He can expose darkness without extinguishing the bruised soul standing in front of Him.
He can say, in effect:
This is sin.
And I am still calling you.
This must die.
And I am offering you life.
Repent.
And come home.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps that is why Matthew 7:1 becomes so dangerous when ripped from its context.
“Judge not” can be abused to silence legitimate biblical correction.
But biblical correction can also be abused to disguise cruelty as courage.
Both distort Jesus.
Some people use Matthew 7:1 because they do not want repentance.
Others ignore Matthew 7:1 because they do not want humility.
Christ confronts both.
Maybe you have been on the receiving end of religious judgment.
Maybe somebody discovered your worst chapter and treated it like the title of your entire life.
Maybe Christians discussed you before anyone prayed with you.
Maybe your divorce became gossip.
Your addiction became entertainment.
Your pregnancy became scandal.
Your failure became a screenshot.
Your past became your name.
People who had never carried your wounds confidently announced what was wrong with you.
And maybe somewhere along the way you began to believe that God looked at you the same way they did.
Please hear this carefully.
Human hypocrisy does not change the character of Jesus Christ.
People may have handled truth without love.
Jesus did not.
People may have exposed you because they enjoyed your humiliation.
Jesus exposes darkness because He calls sinners into light.
People may have wanted your scandal remembered forever.
Jesus went to a cross to accomplish something scandal could never accomplish.
Redemption.
At Calvary, the only truly righteous Judge stepped into the place of the guilty.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so devastating that reconciliation with a holy God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Yet the cross simultaneously announces the staggering depth of divine grace.
Jesus Christ bore sin and judgment so that those who repent and trust in Him can receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
That means Christianity is not a community of people who never needed mercy.
Christianity is supposed to be a community of people who know exactly why mercy matters.
We do not stand above the sinner.
We stand beside the sinner pointing to the Savior.
And sometimes the sinner standing beside us is a brother or sister who needs correction.
Sometimes it is someone who has wandered.
Sometimes it is someone deceived by false teaching.
Sometimes it is somebody trapped in a destructive pattern.
Love does not always remain silent.
If someone you loved were walking toward a cliff in darkness, you would not whisper, “I don't want to judge their journey.”
You would warn them.
But you would warn them because you wanted them alive.
That is the question.
When you confront someone...
do you want restoration, or do you want victory?
When you point out their sin...
do you want them closer to Jesus, or do you want everyone to know you were right?
When someone falls...
does your heart break?
Or does something inside you secretly enjoy watching someone else become smaller?
Be honest.
Because you can defend biblical truth with an unbiblical heart.
You can win an argument while misrepresenting Christ.
You can quote Scripture while feeding pride.
You can identify another person's speck while carrying lumber in your own eye.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needed today.
Not because you should abandon truth.
Because truth should first conquer you.
There is another side to this.
Maybe you are using “judge not” as a shield.
You know what Scripture says.
You know the relationship is dragging you away from Christ.
You know the secret habit is consuming you.
You know your bitterness has become an identity.
You know the compromise is no longer accidental.
But whenever somebody lovingly challenges you, your heart immediately says:
“Who are they to judge me?”
Maybe they are imperfect.
They certainly are.
But an imperfect messenger can still deliver a biblical warning.
The fact that another Christian has flaws does not automatically make every correction false.
So instead of immediately asking, “Who are you to judge me?” perhaps there is a harder question:
Is what they are saying actually true?
Not pleasant.
Not perfectly delivered.
Not convenient.
True.
If it agrees with Scripture, do not let pride make you reject medicine because you dislike the hand holding the cup.
And if someone has confronted you harshly, remember that their harshness does not transform your sin into righteousness.
Take the truth to Jesus.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Examine yourself.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Reject accusations that contradict God’s Word.
But never let another person’s hypocrisy become permission for your own rebellion.
That is freedom.
Not freedom from moral truth.
Freedom from pretending.
Freedom from constantly needing to prove that you are better than somebody else.
Freedom from hiding.
Freedom from condemnation for those who are in Christ.
Freedom to repent because your identity no longer depends upon pretending you have never fallen.
That is where scandal meets grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church was a mess of serious problems.
The Bible does not airbrush human failure.
Yet Scripture repeatedly shows God redeeming people who could never rewrite themselves.
This does not make sin beautiful.
It makes grace astonishing.
And somebody reading this may desperately need to understand the difference.
Your scandal is not your savior.
Your shame is not your savior.
Your church attendance is not your savior.
Your morality is not your savior.
Your ability to identify everybody else’s sin is certainly not your savior.
Jesus Christ is.
The answer to hypocrisy is Jesus.
The answer to self-righteousness is Jesus.
The answer to hidden sin is Jesus.
The answer to condemnation is Jesus.
The answer to the plank and the speck is Jesus.
Come into His light.
Let Him search what you keep defending.
Let Him touch what you keep hiding.
Let Him confront the resentment you renamed discernment.
Let Him confront the compromise you renamed freedom.
Let Him confront the pride you renamed conviction.
And when He exposes something, do not run.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
In Christ, repentance is the road home.
Maybe your prayer today needs to become painfully simple:
“Jesus, show me my plank before I obsess over their speck.”
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian still being rebuilt.

Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because eventually you may need Matthew 7 again—perhaps when someone judges you, perhaps when you are tempted to judge someone else, and perhaps when someone loves you enough to tell you something you desperately do not want to hear.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not as a way to purchase His favor.
Not because giving money somehow makes someone more spiritual.
And before you leave, remember the verse everybody quotes.
“Judge not.”
Now remember what Jesus said next.
Before staring at their speck...
bring your plank to Christ.

Then, when grace has humbled your heart and truth has cleared your vision, you may finally be able to reach toward another wounded sinner—not as their executioner, but as another person who knows where mercy can be found.
Because someday you may discover that the hand you almost raised to condemn someone was the very hand Jesus wanted you to extend to help them home.
Your worst chapter may explain the scars—but Jesus still gets the final word over the story surrendered to Him.
